title: AI Engineering Without Borders — swyx

summary: swyx opens by observing that borders are uniquely human inventions, while AI is a natural "border disrespector" — effortlessly multilingual, natively multimodal with minimal post-training, indifferent to the line between hallucination and memorization, and unconcerned with copyright. He then surveys multiple attempts to define "AI engineer": as someone who works at the API layer, as one of three subtypes (AI-enhanced engineer, AI products engineer, non-human agentic AI engineer), or as a composite job description. He admits none of these are fully satisfying and rejects the cop-out that definitions are purely subjective. He recounts the conference's origin: last year's tracks (RAG, code gen, agents, multimodality) were expanded this year to include open models, evals, inference scaling, enterprise deployment, and AI strategy/management. He confesses these tracks are arbitrary — he invented them from a list of disciplines in the original "Rise of the AI Engineer" document. He contrasts made-up rules with laws of nature that any civilization would independently discover, then asks what the equivalent laws of AI engineering are. He proposes AI engineering sits between software engineering (which omits benefit-to-humanity and natural-law understanding) and traditional engineering. He identifies constants (humans speak 80 wpm but read 200 wpm), contingent facts (Apple Intelligence's 30 tokens/sec becoming a baseline), and trend-driven forces: context window growth from 60-70K tokens to millions, and a 99.55% cost decline for GPT-3-level intelligence. He distinguishes AI engineers from EA and EAC camps by adding a second axis — utility — calling AI engineers "utility maxis." He closes by urging attendees to disrespect borders, disagree productively, and embody the Shoggoth-as-mass-transit mindset: taming forces of nature into useful tools. A brief final sign-off encourages attendees to mingle with one another and expresses swyx's wish to attend in person at the next event.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: AI inherently disrespects human-made borders: it is multilingual, multimodal, blurs hallucination and memorization, and ignores copyright.
No single definition of "AI engineer" is fully settled — API-layer, subtype-based, and job-description approaches all have merit but leave more to explore.
Conference tracks and disciplinary boundaries are arbitrary constructs, not laws of nature; AI engineers should be fluent across all of them.
AI engineering sits between software engineering and traditional engineering, inheriting real-world constraints and a duty to benefit humanity.
Key "Moore's laws of AI" include expanding context windows, improving context utilization, and steeply declining cost of intelligence (99.55% for GPT-3 level).
AI engineers are "utility maxis" — distinct from both EA and EAC camps by prioritizing practical benefit alongside safety and acceleration.
Attendees are urged to productively disagree, cross tracks and disciplines, and resist dogmatic or lazy consensus.
Understand why AI engineering defies traditional disciplinary borders.
Recognize multiple valid but incomplete definitions of the AI engineer role.
Identify key trend lines (context, cost, utilization) that shape AI engineering decisions.

sections.title: Opening: Borders and AI as Border Disrespector
sections.summary: swyx introduces borders as arbitrary human constructs and argues AI inherently disrespects them through multilingualism, multimodality, hallucination/memorization ambiguity, and copyright indifference.

sections.title: Defining the AI Engineer
sections.summary: Reviews three definitional approaches — API-line boundary, three subtypes (AI-enhanced, AI products, non-human agentic), and composite job descriptions — and argues none are conclusive enough to stop exploration.

sections.title: Conference Tracks as Arbitrary Boundaries
sections.summary: Explains the conference's track structure originated from an ad hoc discipline list; swyx admits he made them up and argues such boundaries are not laws of nature.

sections.title: Laws of AI Engineering
sections.summary: Contrasts software engineering (missing natural-law and benefit-of-humanity elements) with traditional engineering; proposes AI engineering sits in between; introduces constants, contingent facts, and trend forces.

sections.title: Moore's Laws of AI and Cost Commodification
sections.summary: Identifies context window expansion (60-70K to millions), context utilization improvements, and steep cost declines (99.55% for GPT-3 level, 80-90% for GPT-4 level) as key trend forces AI engineers should plan around.

sections.title: Philosophy and Closing Message
sections.summary: Positions AI engineers as utility maxis distinct from EA and EAC; urges productive disagreement, border-crossing, and a Shoggoth-as-mass-transit mindset of taming nature into useful tools.

sections.title: Sign-Off
sections.summary: swyx briefly closes, encouraging attendees to mingle, expressing regret at not being present in person, and hoping to see everyone at the next event.

limitations: Proposed "laws of AI engineering" are preliminary and meant to start debate, not conclude it.
Conference tracks are acknowledged as arbitrary and not reflective of how reality must operate.
quantitativeClaims: Humans speak at 80 words per minute but read at 200 words per minute.
Llama can be turned into a visual language model with about $100 of post-training.
MPT-7B had 60,000-70,000 token context windows one year ago; million-token context windows now exist.
Cost of GPT-3-level intelligence declined 99.55% over the past two years.
Cost of GPT-4-level intelligence has come down approximately 80-90%.
Apple Intelligence advertises 30 tokens per second local inference as a baseline.
